disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by intrusive, unwanted thoughts, images, or urges (obsessions) and/or repetitive behaviors or mental acts (compulsions) that the person feels driven to perform. These experiences are time-consuming or cause significant distress and functional impairment, and the individual typically recognizes that their thoughts or behaviors are excessive or unreasonable at some point. The course is often chronic and fluctuating, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress, medical illness, or life transitions. OCD is distinguished from related conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder by the presence of specific, recurrent obsessions and ritualistic responses, and from psychotic disorders by the generally preserved insight and absence of fixed delusional conviction about the intrusive thoughts.

narrative.stressor: Nina’s obsessive tendencies had always blended into her identity as a meticulous designer—double‑checking color codes, reworking layouts late into the night—but they intensified after she shifted to full‑time freelancing five years ago. With no clear boundaries between home and work, she began taking on more community projects than she could comfortably manage, feeling solely responsible for every detail of each brand launch and website publication. A series of tight deadlines and one client’s complaint about a minor printing error left her increasingly preoccupied with the idea that a small oversight in a file could ruin a client’s business and her reputation. Over the past year, this pressure has turned routine projects into exhausting marathons of checking and rechecking, cutting into her gardening, sleep, and ability to deliver work on time; she finally sought psychiatric help after missing a major deadline and realizing she was spending more time stuck in her head than actually designing.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop getting stuck on these awful ‘what if I missed something’ thoughts about my design files, and they’re taking over my workday.”

narrative.stressor: Jason’s long, orderly career in education suited his love of structure, and his quirks about keeping meticulous records and routines were never more than an endearing part of his personality. In the last three years, after his wife developed congestive heart failure and he took on more caregiving responsibilities, his underlying need for control intensified around her medications, diet, and home safety. An episode where she was briefly hospitalized for shortness of breath, despite his careful management, left him with a persistent fear that a single missed step in her care could be catastrophic. As his days became dominated by elaborate, rigid routines around her treatment and the house, he found himself increasingly distressed, exhausted, and unable to focus on his volunteer literacy work, prompting his primary care doctor to refer him for psychiatric evaluation when it became clear his anxiety-driven rituals were interfering with both their quality of life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I have to keep doing the same checks and routines over and over to make sure my wife is safe, and it’s taking up my whole day.”

narrative.stressor: Kennetra’s attention to detail helped her excel when she started her first full‑time bookkeeping job, but the transition from high school and part‑time work to being responsible for real clients’ finances left her feeling a different level of pressure. Around the same time, she moved out of her parents’ home into her own apartment, juggling rent, student loan payments, and expectations she’d set for herself about being a financial role model to the kids she mentors. After a minor error in a spreadsheet at work that was quickly fixed, she became increasingly preoccupied with the idea that she might unknowingly make a serious mistake—either with a client’s accounts or in managing her own bills—that would have irreversible consequences. Over several months, her anxiety about these possibilities grew to the point where it was slowing her down at work, cutting into sleep, and making her late to social and church activities, leading her to seek mental health care when her supervisor gently raised concerns about how long simple tasks were taking her.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My mind keeps getting stuck on these scary ‘what if I mess up the numbers and ruin something’ thoughts, and I can’t turn them off.”
